title: Case Study: Library Management
summary: Design a library system end to end — why one book title needs two classes, search indexing, lending, and fines.

blocks.markdown:
**Design a library management system**: a catalog of book titles, each with multiple physical copies, that lets members search, borrow, return, and reserve books while tracking due dates and fines.

- The single insight that separates a good answer from a naive one: a **title** and a **physical copy** are not the same class.
- Also tests **search design** (by title/author/subject) and a **policy** decision (fines, limits) that must stay easy to change.
- Use [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework) as the general approach; this topic applies it end to end.

blocks.subTitle: Requirements at a glance
blocks.markdown:
What the system must support.

| Capability | Detail |
|---|---|
| Catalog | Titles, each with N physical copies |
| Lending | Borrow, return, due dates, fines |
| Discovery | Search by title, author, subject |
| Fairness | Reservations, max-books-per-member limit |

Every row above becomes a design decision, not just a feature checkbox.

blocks.subTitle: Functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must do:

- Maintain a **catalog** of book titles; each title can have **multiple physical copies**.
- Let members **search** by title, author, or subject.
- **Issue** a copy to a member on borrow, and **accept** it back on return.
- Track a **due date** per loan and compute a **fine** for late returns.
- Let a member **reserve** a title when every copy is currently out, and get notified when one frees up.
- Enforce a **max-books** limit per member so one person can't hoard the catalog.

blocks.subTitle: Non-functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must guarantee, not just do:

- **Search must stay fast** as the catalog grows into the thousands — scanning every title per query won't scale.
- **Availability accuracy** — a copy shown as available must actually be on the shelf, not already checked out.
- **Extensibility** — new fine policies, new search fields, or e-books should slot in without rewriting the lending core.

These shape *how* classes are built, not just which classes exist.

blocks.subTitle: Book vs BookItem — the key insight
blocks.markdown:
**Noun extraction** turns requirements nouns into candidate classes — but "book" hides two different things.

| Noun in requirements | Becomes |
|---|---|
| book title, author, subject | `Book` (the work — one per ISBN) |
| physical copy, barcode, shelf | `BookItem` (one per copy, can be borrowed) |
| member, librarian, loan, reservation | `Member`, `Librarian`, `Lending`, `Reservation` |

A **title** is metadata shared by every copy; a **copy** is a physical object with its own status. Merging them into one `Book` class breaks the moment a title has more than one copy.

The classes above, wired together:

- **Composition** (filled diamond): a `Book` owns its `BookItem` copies — delete the title, the copies go with it.
- `Lending` is the join between a `Member` and a specific `BookItem`, not the `Book` — you borrow a copy, not a title.

blocks.subTitle: Book vs BookItem
blocks.markdown:
`Book` is shared metadata for a title. `BookItem` is one physical, borrowable copy of it.

```text
class Book:
    isbn: String
    title: String
    author: String
    subject: String
    publisher: String

    constructor(isbn, title, author, subject, publisher):
        this.isbn = isbn
        this.title = title
        this.author = author
        this.subject = subject
        this.publisher = publisher

enum ItemStatus:
    AVAILABLE
    LOANED
    RESERVED
    LOST

class BookItem:
    barcode: String
    book: Book              // which title this copy belongs to
    status: ItemStatus = AVAILABLE
    rackLocation: String

    method isAvailable(): boolean:
        return status == ItemStatus.AVAILABLE

    method checkout():
        if not isAvailable():
            throw ItemNotAvailableException()
        status = ItemStatus.LOANED

    method returnItem():
        status = ItemStatus.AVAILABLE
```

blocks.subTitle: Member & Librarian
blocks.markdown:
Both are people who interact with the system, but only one borrows books — they get separate classes because their allowed actions differ.

```text
abstract class Account:
    id: String
    name: String
    email: String

class Member extends Account:
    booksBorrowed: List<Lending> = []
    maxBooksAllowed: int = 5

    method canBorrow(): boolean:
        return booksBorrowed.size() < maxBooksAllowed

    method totalFinesDue(): Money:
        return booksBorrowed
            .map(l -> l.calculateFine())
            .sum()

class Librarian extends Account:
    method addBookItem(book: Book, barcode: String): BookItem:
        item = new BookItem(barcode, book)
        catalog.addItem(item)
        return item

    method issueBook(item: BookItem, member: Member): Lending:
        return lendingService.checkout(item, member)
```

blocks.subTitle: Catalog & search
Lending — issue and return
blocks.markdown:
`Lending` (a.k.a. `BookLending`) is the record of one member holding one copy — it exists from checkout until return, and holds the dates the fine math depends on.

```text
class Lending:
    bookItem: BookItem
    member: Member
    issueDate: Date
    dueDate: Date
    returnDate: Date = null

    constructor(bookItem, member, issueDate, loanDays):
        this.bookItem = bookItem
        this.member = member
        this.issueDate = issueDate
        this.dueDate = issueDate.plusDays(loanDays)

class LendingService:
    method checkout(item: BookItem, member: Member): Lending:
        if not item.isAvailable():
            throw ItemNotAvailableException()
        if not member.canBorrow():
            throw MaxBooksLimitReachedException()
        item.checkout()
        lending = new Lending(item, member, today(), loanDays = 14)
        member.booksBorrowed.add(lending)
        return lending

    method returnBook(lending: Lending): Money:
        lending.returnDate = today()
        lending.bookItem.returnItem()
        fine = lending.calculateFine()
        lending.member.booksBorrowed.remove(lending)
        reservationService.notifyIfReserved(lending.bookItem.book)
        return fine
```

blocks.subTitle: Fine calculation
Reservation
blocks.markdown:
A reservation is on the **title**, not a specific copy — the member doesn't care which physical copy they get, only that one becomes free.

```text
class Reservation:
    book: Book
    member: Member
    reservedAt: DateTime

class ReservationService:
    private queueByBook: Map<Book, Queue<Reservation>> = {}

    method reserve(book: Book, member: Member): Reservation:
        r = new Reservation(book, member, now())
        queueByBook.putQueue(book, r)   // FIFO — first to reserve, first served
        return r

    method notifyIfReserved(book: Book):
        queue = queueByBook.get(book)
        if queue != null and not queue.isEmpty():
            next = queue.dequeue()
            notificationService.notify(next.member, book)
```

Where each decision and pattern earns its place:

| Decision / pattern | Why |
|---|---|
| Book vs BookItem split | Title metadata is shared; copy status is per-instance |
| Indexed `Catalog` (not linear scan) | Search stays fast as the catalog grows |
| Strategy (search/fine rules) | Swap ranking or fine policy without touching `Lending` |
| Observer (`notifyIfReserved`) | `Member`s subscribe to a title's availability, decoupled from checkout code |

See [object-relationships](object-relationships) for composition vs association, and [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i) for Strategy and Observer in general form.

Cases a naive design misses:

- **Lost book** — marking an item `LOST` (not just deleting it) preserves loan history and lets the library charge a replacement fee instead of silently losing the record.
- **Fine never paid off** — without a `totalFinesDue()` check, a member could keep borrowing while owing money; `canBorrow()` should also check fines, not just the count.
- **Max-books limit counted wrong** — counting active `Lending` records (not a manually incremented counter) avoids drift if a return fails partway through.

How the design absorbs real follow-up requirements without a rewrite:

- **E-books** — add an `EBookItem` with no `rackLocation` and unlimited concurrent "copies"; `Book` and `Catalog` need no changes.
- **Multiple branches** — add a `Branch` that owns a subset of `BookItem`s; search stays catalog-wide, availability becomes branch-scoped.
- **Trade-off**: three separate search indexes cost memory and must stay in sync on every write — fine for a library-scale catalog, but a full-text search engine would replace them at web scale.

blocks.subTitle: Why separate Book from BookItem
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why do you need both a `Book` and a `BookItem` class?**

`Book` holds title-level metadata (author, ISBN, subject) that's identical across every copy. `BookItem` holds per-copy state — barcode, shelf location, and status (available/loaned/lost) — that differs copy to copy. Merging them forces you to either duplicate title metadata per copy or pretend a title only ever has one copy; splitting them lets one `Book` cleanly own many `BookItem`s.

blocks.subTitle: Supporting search by multiple fields
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you support search by title, author, and subject efficiently?**

Maintain a separate index map per searchable field — title, author, subject — each mapping a lowercased key to the list of matching `Book`s. A write (adding a book) updates all three maps once; a read (a search) is then an O(1) map lookup instead of scanning the whole catalog. This is the same idea as a database index, just built by hand in memory.

blocks.subTitle: Computing fines
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you compute a fine for a late return?**

Store `dueDate` on the `Lending` at checkout. On return (or on demand, before return), compute `lateDays = max(0, daysBetween(dueDate, returnDate ?? today()))` and multiply by a per-day rate. Falling back to `today()` when `returnDate` is still null lets a member see their running fine before they've returned the book, and keeping the rate as a single constant (or a swappable strategy) means finance can change it without touching the lending logic.

blocks.subTitle: Handling reservations
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you handle reservations when all copies are checked out?**

A member reserves the `Book` (the title), not a specific `BookItem`, since they don't care which physical copy they get. Keep a FIFO queue of reservations per book. When any copy of that title is returned, dequeue the earliest reservation and hand that member first claim — typically by holding the copy for them briefly before it goes back to general availability.

blocks.subTitle: Notifying members of availability
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How would you notify members when a reserved book becomes available?**

This is the **Observer** pattern: a reservation is effectively a subscription to a book's availability event. When `LendingService.returnBook()` runs, it calls `notifyIfReserved(book)`, which checks that book's reservation queue and pushes a notification to the next member in line — the checkout code never needs to know notifications exist, it just fires the event.

blocks.subTitle: Why not one Book class with a copy count
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why not just give `Book` a `copiesAvailable` integer instead of a `BookItem` class?**

A plain counter can't tell you *which* copy a member has, so you can't track per-copy condition, shelf location, or mark one specific copy `LOST` without corrupting the count for the rest. `BookItem` gives every physical copy its own identity and lifecycle, which a counter fundamentally can't represent — the count then falls out naturally as `items.filter(isAvailable).size()`.
